unit roundoff.d: The largest relative error made when one real number is rounded to a floating-point format: about 6×10⁻⁸ in fp32, 1.1×10⁻¹⁶ in fp64 and 3.9×10⁻³ in bf16.

truncation error.d: The error from cutting a Taylor series short, for example in a finite difference. It shrinks as the step shrinks (like ε for a forward difference, like ε² for a central one).

catastrophic cancellation.d: Losing almost all significant digits by subtracting two nearly equal rounded numbers. Example: weighing a lorry before and after a pigeon lands, on a scale that reads to 10 kg. It is why a finite-difference step cannot be made arbitrarily small.

mantissa.d: The part of a floating-point number that holds its significant digits (the other parts are the sign and the exponent). fp32 keeps 23 fraction bits, bf16 only 7.

reverse-over-reverse.d: Computing a Hessian-vector product by taking the gradient, dotting it with v, and backpropagating a second time. Gives the same exact result as forward-over-reverse; it is what the project's hvp.py does.

upcast.d: Convert a number to a format with more digits, e.g. bf16 to fp32. This is exact: every bf16 number is an fp32 number with its last 16 bits set to zero.

backward-equivalent.d: A unit of compute cost used in theory-v2: one backward pass (one vector-Jacobian product) through the full depth of the model for one sequence.

TF32.d: A reduced-precision mode some GPUs use to speed up fp32 matrix products, keeping only about as many fraction bits as fp16. The project's HVPs ran in fp32 with it switched off.
